citation.title: Deep Generative Design: Integration of Topology Optimization and Generative Models
citation.authors: Sangeun Oh, Yongsu Jung, Seongsin Kim, Ikjin Lee, Namwoo Kang
citation.venue: Journal of Mechanical Design 141(11), 111405 (arXiv journal reference); arXiv preprint (cs.LG; also cs.CE, cs.NE). A first-page note says an earlier version was presented at ASME IDETC 2018
citation.version_coded: arXiv v2 (20 May 2019; v1 1 Mar 2019), PDF, 22 pages; its header marks it as the manuscript submitted to JMD. The arXiv HTML returned 404. The ASME version of record returned HTTP 403 to scripted access and was not read

included.reason: I-QUALITY (screened I-UNCLEAR; the only classical comparison is a qualitative diversity comparison with TO-only exploration, Sec. 7.1, Figs. 13-14; no runtime of any method is compared)

claim.primary_outcome_paraphrase: The TO-plus-GAN framework is claimed to yield more aesthetic, diverse and robust wheel designs than earlier generative-design methods; the supporting classical runs are qualitative: TO without reference designs gives near-identical or unconverged results (Sec. 7.1).
claim.key_phrase: better aesthetics, diversity, and robustness of generated designs than previous generative design methods
claim.location: Abstract (qualitative; §5.1 rule 3, because no quantitative comparison of the learned model with a classical method exists anywhere); supporting classical runs in Section 7.1, Figs. 13-14 (pp. 16-17)
claim.claimed_speedup_basis: No runtime of TO or of the GAN is compared. Only BEGAN training time is given (about 3 h on four GTX 1080 GPUs, Sec. 6.1.2). Not derivable.
claim.alternatives: (1) Sec. 8 conclusion: more diverse designs than conventional generative design (qualitative), and better robustness than plain generative models, which suffer mode collapse (an ML comparison). (2) Sec. 7.1, Fig. 14: iterative TO-only exploration from 4 TO references gives similar designs (qualitative). (3) Table 2: compliance of TO with market reference designs vs plain TO (similarity 0): 5.28 vs 5.23–9.28 (design A) and 8.88 vs 8.90–13.02 (design B); this measures the trade-off of the similarity term, with no learned model involved. (4) Sec. 7.2: BEGAN vs DCGAN and VAE (ML only). (5) Sec. 7.3: autoencoder novelty classifier with precision and recall 91.6% (ML only).

baseline.classical_method: Three-field SIMP compliance minimization with OC updates, density filter and Heaviside projection (Sec. 4.1). Classical baseline for the claim: TO without reference designs at 5 force ratios (Fig. 13) and iterative TO-only exploration that reuses TO results as references (Fig. 14)
baseline.implementation: authors' MATLAB code built on the 99- and 88-line educational codes (Sec. 4.1.1, 4.2)
baseline.hardware_classical: not stated (TO runs executed in parallel, Sec. 6.1.1)
baseline.hardware_ml: four GTX 1080 GPUs for BEGAN training (Sec. 6.1.2)
baseline.problem_size: 128×128 elements; 2D wheel with a non-design rim and a fixed hub (Sec. 4.2)
baseline.classical_iterations: not stated; convergence when the design change falls below a tolerance described as typically 0.01 (Eq. 7); the value used is not stated
baseline.training_time: about 3 h on four GTX 1080 GPUs for BEGAN (Sec. 6.1.2); autoencoder training time not stated
baseline.data_generation_cost: not stated; iteration 1: 658 web-crawled wheel images × 25 condition pairs [derived: up to 16,450 TO runs], 1,619 kept; iteration 2: 128 GAN references × 25 [derived: up to 3,200 TO runs], 385 kept (rule of Sec. 4.2 with Table 1; Table 3)
baseline.quality_metric: No diversity or aesthetics metric is computed for the classical comparison. The framework counts new designs after pixel-wise L1 filtering (threshold 10^3, Sec. 3), scores novelty by autoencoder reconstruction error and reports compliance and cost of the TO outputs (Fig. 11)
baseline.quality_gap: Qualitative only: without reference designs TO returns the same optimum for fixed boundary conditions and does not converge for two of five force ratios (Fig. 13a-b); TO-only iteration yields similar designs (Fig. 14). The framework yields 2,004 new designs after two iterations (Table 3)

R1.evidence: Sec. 7.1, Figs. 13-14, Sec. 4.2 and Table 3: the diversity comparison is qualitative and not budget-matched. The framework runs TO for 658 market references × 25 condition pairs [derived: up to 16,450 runs] and 128 GAN references × 25 [derived: up to 3,200 runs], plus about 3 h of BEGAN training (Sec. 6.1.2). The TO-only baseline shows 5 runs without references (Fig. 13) and 12 selected results from 4 TO references (Fig. 14) [counted from the figure]; the number of baseline runs and the stopping tolerance used are not stated. No diversity metric is computed for the baseline.

R2.evidence: Sec. 4.1-4.2 and 7.1: the classical engine is the authors' three-field SIMP code (OC, density filter, Heaviside projection) built on the 99- and 88-line MATLAB codes, the same engine used inside the framework, on 128×128 elements. The TO-only baseline varies only the force ratio (5 levels) from a uniform start; the authors report that it does not converge for two force ratios (Fig. 13a-b) and that reusing TO outputs as references gives similar designs (Fig. 14). A broader classical exploration (varying supports, volume fraction or initial designs) is not tried [inferred]. No runtimes exist, so markers (a)-(e) cannot apply. Unsure, so pass.

R3.evidence: Quality stratum; no speed or cost claim against TO. For C3: BEGAN training about 3 h on four GTX 1080 GPUs (Sec. 6.1.2); TO run counts as derived under R1; TO run times are not reported.

R4.evidence: All final designs are TO outputs, so their compliance and cost come from FE-based optimization (Fig. 11 for 2,004 designs; Table 2). But the claimed advantage (aesthetics, diversity) is judged from images: pixel-wise L1 filtering (threshold 10^3, Sec. 3) and visual examples (Figs. 7, 10, 13-14); aesthetics is assumed from market designs, not measured (Sec. 3, Stage 2). Rejection counts are not reported: neither the number of GAN samples before Stage-6 filtering nor any non-converged TO runs inside the framework. Fig. 14 states its selection rule (the most different results); Fig. 10 does not. A strict reading (image metric only) gives fail.

reporting.n_test_cases: One 2D wheel problem (128×128); 2,004 generated designs after two iterations (Table 3); classical comparison: 5 TO runs without references (Fig. 13) and 12 selected TO-only results from 4 references (Fig. 14) [counted from the figure]

notes: Screening code was I-UNCLEAR. Inclusion judgment: the article runs a classical method and reports its results (TO without reference designs, Figs. 13-14), so the FT-NOBASELINE clarification does not apply; the comparison is qualitative. Scope judgment for the verifier: the GAN only proposes reference shapes, and every final design is a classical TO output (Stage 2, Sec. 3). If §3.1 is read as requiring the learned model to produce, accelerate or replace the TO result itself, FT-SCOPE applies. Primary outcome: the Abstract compares with earlier generative-design methods, which Sec. 1.1 describes as TO-based design exploration [inferred to be the classical comparator]; its robustness part refers to generative models (Sec. 1.2, Sec. 8), an ML comparison. Possible inconsistency: Sec. 4.2 defines the force ratio as normal over shear force, but Sec. 7.1 attributes the non-converged runs at ratios 0 and 0.1 to the absence of shear force. Aesthetics is assumed from market designs (Sec. 3, Stage 2) and never measured. The L1 threshold of 10^3 was checked on the rendered PDF page 5. hardware_per_method_stated = partial: GPUs are given for BEGAN only. No code or data statement in arXiv v2. retest_candidate false: quality stratum, qualitative claim, no public code.
